title.full: Canada’s Energy Future 2026: Energy Supply and Demand Projections to 2050

description: Normative pathway to economy-wide net-zero GHG in Canada by 2050.
pathwayDescription:
Canada Net-zero assumes net-zero GHG emissions in Canada by 2050 and explores one possible pathway to reach this. THE CRE raises policy stringency orderly: an aggregate carbon cost reaching $550/t, tighter clean fuel rules, a freight ZEV standard, net-zero buildings and offsets for negative emissions. It also assumes faster rest-of-world climate action (outcomes closer to 2°C), which lowers oil and gas prices, and clean-technology cost declines 20–60% larger than in Current Measures. Electricity demand more than doubles, electricity reaches about 35% of end-use energy demand, and residual emissions are offset by BECCS, direct air capture and land-based removals.

The CER is in charge of regulating construction and operation of energy assets and transport, export and trade of energy, exploration and siting activities. One of its responsibilities is to provide fact-based information on energy markets and supply as part of the Energy Information Program.

coreDrivers.policies: More stringent measures are adopted than in Current Measures: carbon tax continues to rise and reaches $450/t in 2050. Freight ZEV standard targets MDV and HDV sales to be 100% ZEV by 2040; 40–45% clean fuels in marine and aviation; no new oil heating from 2030 or gas heating from 2035; enhanced methane rules (−75% by 2030); and paid offsets for negative emissions.
coreDrivers.emissionsTargets: Net-zero GHG emissions for Canada in 2050 is a predetermined constraint: policy stringency is raised iteratively until modelled net emissions reach zero (−0.01 Mt CO2e in 2050), with residual emissions offset by BECCS, DAC, land-use and nature-based removals.
coreDrivers.technologyCosts: Clean-technology costs fall 20–60% further than in Current Measures (faster global deployment): 2024–2050 onshore wind  decrease by 40%, utility solar by 54%, SMR by 50%, and electrolysis  by 62%. Lower costs keep electricity prices the lowest of all scenarios despite the highest demand and support much higher deplyoment of onshore wind, SMR, and BECCS than Current Measures. Cost sensitivity of CCUS could cut oil sands output further.
coreDrivers.macroeconomicDrivers: GDP grows 1.5%/yr, marginally below Current Measures because lower upstream oil and gas activity is partly offset by stronger clean-technology investment; population growth (0.7%/yr) matches Current Measures. Macro trends are secondary here to the net-zero constraint and policy.
coreDrivers.otherDrivers: Assumed faster rest-of-world climate action (closer to 2°C) lowers global oil and gas demand: Brent falls to ~US$65/bbl by 2050 and Henry Hub stays at $4.00. One additional LNG project and 3.5GW of data center load are needed by 2050.

dependencies.dependency_description: Net-negative power emissions (−37 Mt in 2050) depend on policy beyond current law: an aggregate cost of carbon reaching $450/t and an assumed offset system paying negative-emission providers (BECCS, DAC) at that rate. Without that compensation BECCS, which delivers the negative emissions, has no revenue basis. Current Clean Electricity Regulations and ITCs also apply.

Beyond the Clean Electricity Regulations, the pathway needs a new regulatory market for negative-emission offsets (crediting BECCS and DAC removals) and approvals for CO2 transport and storage serving 8.9 GW gas-CCUS and 5.5 GW BECCS. The report assumes this ‘robust system exists’ rather than modelling how it is created.

Around $46 bn/year of investment is needed, but lower clean-technology capital costs make Canada Net-zero’s electricity prices the lowest of all scenarios, rising slower than inflation. The economics hinge on the aggregate carbon cost and paid offsets that reward BECCS. 2024–2050 capex assumptions are 20–60% below Current Measures.

The report does not model opposition. 149 GW of new onshore wind, 11.3 GW of SMRs and BECCS with CO2 storage imply the greatest siting footprint; the report’s Indigenous engagement stresses ownership, FPIC and minimising ecosystem and cultural impacts as conditions for community support.

Electrification of heating (heat pumps) and freight is driven by mandates and costs, not modelled preferences; power demand more than doubles. Excluded demand-side management is flagged as a potential way to reduce peak load in the high-renewable Canada Net-zero system.

With 40% wind in generation technology mix, generation more than doubling and 29 GW of batteries, interties (~70% more capacity, flows to ~140 TWh) and storage are essential to reliability; BECCS and gas-CCUS also need CO2 transport and storage networks. The report highlights flexibility as most important in Canada Net-zero. Canada–US transfer capacity is held constant.

Net-negative power requires BECCS (5.5 GW, 40 TWh) not yet deployed in Canada, alongside 11.3 GW SMR (twice the capacity built in Current Measure, but less than in Higher Demand), 8.9 GW gas-CCUS and 29 GW batteries (23% more than in Current Measure), with capex assumed 20–60% below Current Measures (SMR $6,187/kW by 2050). The High CCUS Cost sensitivity shows CCUS cost uncertainty is material to the pathway.

The largest build needs 565 kt copper, 126 kt graphite, 12 kt lithium and 1.0 kt dysprosium (2025–2050) from concentrated supply chains, and BECCS draws on domestic biomass residues and crops plus imported biofuels competing with transport fuels.

With wind representing 40% of generation technology mix and electrified heating, rare cold, low-wind events drive the flexibility need, which the report flags as greatest in Canada Net-zero. Hydro output would also vary with precipitation but the models do not otherwise include climate-change impacts.

Around $46 bn/yr of spending and the most novel technologies (BECCS, SMRs, CCUS) raise demand for specialised skills. The report warns shortages could affect timelines and costs, but doesn't quantify it.

byMetric.scopeLimitations: Electricity economic-sector GHG, Mt CO2e, national only (no provincial split). Residual unabated gas runs under Clean Electricity Regulations compliance flexibility (p.51). Includes BECCS negative emissions (−37.4 Mt in 2050).

Installed capacity MW, Canada and provinces. Storage is battery only (‘Battery Storage’); pumped hydro is not separated and appears to sit within Hydro. No info on if captive or rooftop capacities are included in analysis. Includes wind dedicated to hydrogen production.

Derived: electricity-sector Mt CO2e (national inventory basis, direct, CO2e) ÷ total generation incl. distributed solar and wind dedicated to hydrogen; captive industrial generation not separately identified, so numerator and denominator may not align. Negative from ~2050 as BECCS outweighs residual gas emissions.
Generation GWh, Canada and provinces; includes distributed solar and wind dedicated to electrolysis. No info on if captive or rooftop capacities are included in analysis.
Capital and repair expenditure, C$2025, bulk power system only; excludes distribution and transmission other than generation connections and interties (p.88).
Overnight capital costs for onshore wind, utility solar, NG with CCUS and SMR; no storage, hydro or O&M costs disclosed; no cost file in the Open Government dataset.
Derived share of generation by technology (each technology ÷ ‘Total’); boundary as Generation.

Transfer capacity only stated in prose (~70% more interprovincial capacity by 2050 in all scenarios). Annual flows (not lines) are in electricity-interchange-2026.csv. Canada–US capacity fixed; distribution excluded.
